subject: mathematics
name: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round
summary: This is the chapter on circles. It covers the parts of a circle (centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc, segment, sector), how many circles pass through given points, the circumcentre of a triangle, the properties of chords, the angles that arcs subtend at the centre and on the circle, and cyclic quadrilaterals.

topics.title: Circles and their parts
topics.summary: A circle is the set of all points at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre); chords, arcs, segments and sectors are its parts.
topics.simple: A **circle** is all the points that are the same distance from one middle point, the **centre**. That distance is the **radius**. A line joining two points on the circle is a **chord**, and the longest chord, through the centre, is the **diameter** (twice the radius).
topics.explain:
A **circle** is the set of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance from a fixed point.
- The fixed point is the **centre** (usually called O).
- The fixed distance is the **radius** (r). All radii of a circle are equal.
- The **circumference** is the length of the boundary of the circle.

**Chord:** a line segment joining any two points on the circle.
**Diameter:** a chord passing through the centre. Diameter = 2 × radius, and it is the **longest chord** of a circle.

**Arc:** a part of the circle between two points on it. Two points divide the circle into two arcs:
- the **minor arc** (the shorter one)
- the **major arc** (the longer one)
- if the two points are ends of a diameter, both arcs are **semicircles**.

**Segment:** the region between a chord and an arc. The smaller one is the **minor segment**, the larger one is the **major segment**.

**Sector:** the region between two radii and an arc, shaped like a slice of pizza (minor sector and major sector).

**Symmetry:** a circle looks the same after any rotation about its centre, and **every line through the centre (every diameter) is a line of symmetry**. So a circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.

The interior of the circle is the set of points closer to the centre than r; the exterior is the set of points farther than r.
topics.example: A bangle has a diameter of 6 cm. Its radius is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm. The segment made by a cut across a round roti (not through the centre) is a minor segment on one side and a major segment on the other.
keyPoints: Circle: all points at distance r from the centre
Diameter = 2r; it is the longest chord
Minor arc is shorter, major arc is longer; a diameter gives two semicircles
Segment = region between chord and arc
Sector = region between two radii and an arc
Every diameter is a line of symmetry — infinitely many

topics.title: Circles through given points and the circumcentre
topics.summary: Infinitely many circles pass through one point or two points, but exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points; its centre is the circumcentre of the triangle they form.
topics.simple: Through one point you can draw endless circles. Through two points you can still draw endless circles, but their centres all lie on one line — the perpendicular bisector of the two points. Through three points that are not on one line, there is **exactly one** circle.
topics.explain:
**One point P:** take any centre and use its distance to P as the radius. So **infinitely many** circles pass through one point.

**Two points A and B:** the centre must be equally far from A and B, so it must lie on the **perpendicular bisector of AB**. Every point on that line works, so **infinitely many** circles pass through A and B. The smallest one has AB as its diameter.

**Three non-collinear points A, B, C:** the centre must lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB **and** on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Two non-parallel lines meet in exactly one point, so there is **exactly one** circle.

**Three collinear points:** the perpendicular bisectors are parallel and never meet, so **no** circle passes through them.

**Circumcentre and circumcircle:** the circle through the three vertices of a triangle is its **circumcircle**. Its centre, the **circumcentre**, is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet. Its position depends on the type of triangle:
- **Acute triangle:** circumcentre lies **inside** the triangle
- **Right triangle:** circumcentre is the **midpoint of the hypotenuse**
- **Obtuse triangle:** circumcentre lies **outside** the triangle
topics.example: A right triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm (6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10²). Its circumcentre is the midpoint of the 10 cm hypotenuse, so the circumradius is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
keyPoints: 1 point → infinitely many circles
2 points → infinitely many circles, centres on the perpendicular bisector
3 non-collinear points → exactly one circle
3 collinear points → no circle
Circumcentre = meeting point of perpendicular bisectors of the sides
Acute: inside; right: midpoint of hypotenuse; obtuse: outside

topics.title: Properties of chords
topics.summary: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre and are equidistant from it; the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord; chord length = 2√(r² − d²).
topics.simple: Chords of the same length behave the same way: they make the same angle at the centre and are the same distance from the centre. A line from the centre that hits a chord at 90° cuts it exactly in half. These facts let you find chord lengths using Pythagoras.
topics.explain:
Each of these results has a **converse** that is also true (in the same circle or in equal circles).

**1. Chords and angles at the centre**
- Equal chords subtend **equal angles at the centre**.
- Converse: if two chords subtend equal angles at the centre, the chords are equal.
- Proof idea: joining the ends of each chord to O gives two triangles that are congruent by SSS (two radii and the equal chord).

**2. Perpendicular from the centre**
- The perpendicular from the centre to a chord **bisects** the chord.
- Converse: the line from the centre to the **midpoint** of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
- Proof idea: if OM ⊥ AB, triangles OMA and OMB are congruent by RHS (OA = OB, OM common), so AM = MB.

**3. Distance from the centre**
- Equal chords are **equidistant** from the centre.
- Converse: chords equidistant from the centre are equal.
- The closer a chord is to the centre, the longer it is; the diameter (distance 0) is the longest.

**Chord length formula:** if a chord is at distance d from the centre of a circle of radius r, the perpendicular from O makes a right triangle with hypotenuse r and legs d and half the chord. By Pythagoras, half-chord = √(r² − d²), so
**chord length = 2√(r² − d²)**.
topics.example:
Radius r = 5 cm, chord at distance d = 3 cm from the centre.
1. Half-chord = √(5² − 3²) = √(25 − 9) = √16 = 4 cm
2. Chord = 2 × 4 = **8 cm**

Reverse problem: a chord of length 24 cm in a circle of radius 13 cm. Half-chord = 12, so d = √(13² − 12²) = √(169 − 144) = √25 = **5 cm**.
keyPoints: Equal chords ⇔ equal angles at the centre
Perpendicular from centre bisects the chord (and converse)
Equal chords ⇔ equidistant from the centre
Nearer the centre means longer chord; diameter is longest
Chord length = 2√(r² − d²)

topics.title: Angles subtended by arcs
topics.summary: The angle an arc subtends at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle; angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is 90°.
topics.simple: Take an arc and join its ends to the centre, and also to a point on the rest of the circle. The angle at the centre is always **twice** the angle at the circle. That's why all angles standing on the same arc are equal, and why any angle drawn in a semicircle is exactly 90°.
topics.explain:
An arc PQ **subtends** an angle ∠POQ at the centre O, and an angle ∠PRQ at any point R on the remaining part of the circle.

**Theorem (double angle):** ∠POQ = 2 × ∠PRQ.

Proof idea: join R to O and extend it. Triangles OPR and OQR are isosceles (OP = OR = OQ), so the base angles are equal. The exterior angle of each triangle at O equals twice the base angle. Adding (or subtracting) the two parts gives ∠POQ = 2∠PRQ.

**Consequences:**
- **Angles in the same segment are equal.** Every point R on the same arc gives ∠PRQ = ½∠POQ, the same value.
- **Angle in a semicircle is 90°.** If PQ is a diameter, ∠POQ = 180°, so ∠PRQ = 180° ÷ 2 = 90°.
- Conversely, if a segment PQ subtends 90° at R, then R lies on the circle with PQ as diameter.

**Concyclic points:** points that lie on the same circle. If a segment AB subtends equal angles at two points C and D on the same side of AB, then A, B, C and D are concyclic.
topics.example:
An arc subtends 110° at the centre. At any point on the remaining part of the circle it subtends 110° ÷ 2 = **55°**.

In a circle, AB is a diameter and C is on the circle with ∠CAB = 35°. Since ∠ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle), ∠CBA = 180° − 90° − 35° = **55°**.
keyPoints: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at the circle (same arc)
Angles in the same segment are equal
Angle in a semicircle = 90°
Equal angles on the same side of a segment ⇒ the four points are concyclic
Concyclic = lying on one circle

topics.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
topics.summary: A quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on a circle is cyclic; its opposite angles add up to 180°, and any exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.
topics.simple: If all four corners of a quadrilateral sit on one circle, it is **cyclic**. In such a quadrilateral, opposite angles always add up to 180°. If the opposite angles of a quadrilateral add to 180°, you can draw a circle through its corners.
topics.explain:
A **cyclic quadrilateral** is one whose four vertices are concyclic (lie on one circle).

**Theorem:** the sum of either pair of **opposite angles** of a cyclic quadrilateral is **180°**.
- ∠A + ∠C = 180° and ∠B + ∠D = 180°
- Proof idea: ∠A and ∠C stand on the two arcs that make up the whole circle. Their central angles add up to 360°, and each inscribed angle is half its central angle, so ∠A + ∠C = 360° ÷ 2 = 180°.

**Converse:** if a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180°, the quadrilateral is cyclic.

**Exterior angle:** if one side of a cyclic quadrilateral is extended, the **exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle**. (Exterior angle at C = 180° − ∠C = ∠A.)

**Which parallelograms are cyclic?** In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal. For it to be cyclic they must also add to 180°, so each must be 90°. Hence **the only cyclic parallelograms are rectangles** (including squares). A rhombus that is not a square is not cyclic.

An **isosceles trapezium** is also always cyclic, because its base angles make opposite angles supplementary.
topics.example:
ABCD is cyclic with ∠A = 110° and ∠B = 75°.
- ∠C = 180° − 110° = **70°**
- ∠D = 180° − 75° = **105°**
- Check: 110° + 75° + 70° + 105° = 360° ✓
- If side DC is extended beyond C, the exterior angle at C = ∠A = 110°.
keyPoints: Cyclic quadrilateral: all four vertices on one circle
Opposite angles add up to 180°
Converse: opposite angles supplementary ⇒ cyclic
Exterior angle = interior opposite angle
Only rectangles (and squares) are cyclic parallelograms
Isosceles trapezium is cyclic

keyConcepts.meaning: The set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance (radius) from a fixed point (centre).
A line segment joining two points on a circle.
A chord through the centre; equal to 2r and the longest chord.
A part of the circle between two points; minor arc is shorter, major arc is longer.
The region between a chord and its arc.
The region between two radii and the arc between them.
The line at 90° through the midpoint of a segment; every point on it is equidistant from the ends.
The point where the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle's sides meet; centre of the circle through its vertices.
The angle formed at a point by lines drawn to the two ends of a chord or arc.
Points that all lie on one circle.
A quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on a circle; its opposite angles add to 180°.

Angle at centre = 2 × angle at any point on the remaining part of the circle (same arc)
Exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral = interior opposite angle
commonMistakes: Saying only one circle passes through two points — infinitely many do; you need three non-collinear points for exactly one.
Forgetting that three collinear points have no circle through them.
Halving the wrong way: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle, not half.
Using the chord length directly in Pythagoras — use half the chord: (chord/2)² + d² = r².
Saying opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal — they are supplementary (add to 180°).
Thinking every parallelogram is cyclic — only rectangles (and squares) are.
Placing the circumcentre of a right triangle at the right-angle vertex — it is at the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

Every diameter is a line of symmetry: a circle has infinitely many.

Centres of circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

Angle at centre = 2 × angle at the circle on the same arc.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a segment and a sector?
faqs.a: A **segment** is bounded by a **chord** and an arc. A **sector** is bounded by **two radii** and an arc. A sector always has the centre as a corner; a segment usually does not.

faqs.q: Why is the angle in a semicircle always 90°?
faqs.a: The diameter subtends a straight angle of **180°** at the centre. The angle at any point on the circle is half the angle at the centre, so it is 180° ÷ 2 = **90°**.

faqs.q: How many circles can pass through two points? Through three points?
faqs.a: Through two points, **infinitely many** — their centres lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Through three **non-collinear** points, **exactly one**. Through three collinear points, **none**.

faqs.q: How do I find the length of a chord if I know the radius and its distance from the centre?
faqs.a: Draw the perpendicular from the centre; it bisects the chord. Then half-chord = √(r² − d²), so chord = 2√(r² − d²). For r = 5 and d = 3: 2√(25 − 9) = 2 × 4 = **8**.
No. A parallelogram has equal opposite angles; to be cyclic they must also add to 180°, so each must be 90°. So only **rectangles** (including squares) are cyclic parallelograms.

quiz.q: The longest chord of a circle is its:
quiz.explain: A diameter passes through the centre and is the longest chord (2r).

quiz.q: The region between a chord and its arc is called a:
quiz.explain: A segment is bounded by a chord and an arc; a sector by two radii and an arc.

quiz.q: How many circles pass through three non-collinear points?
quiz.explain: The perpendicular bisectors of two sides meet at exactly one point — the only possible centre.

quiz.q: Where is the circumcentre of a right-angled triangle?
options: At the midpoint of the hypotenuse
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle (angle in a semicircle is 90°), so the centre is its midpoint.

quiz.q: A chord is 3 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Its length is:
A chord of length 24 cm is in a circle of radius 13 cm. How far is it from the centre?
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord:
options: Is always equal to the radius
quiz.explain: By RHS congruence the two halves of the chord are equal.

quiz.q: An arc subtends 80° at the centre. What angle does it subtend at a point on the remaining part of the circle?
quiz.explain: The angle at the circle is half the angle at the centre: 80° ÷ 2 = 40°.

quiz.q: AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle with ∠CAB = 35°. Find ∠CBA.
In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 110°. What is ∠C?
quiz.explain: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°: 180° − 110° = 70°.

quiz.q: Which of these parallelograms is always cyclic?
quiz.explain: Equal opposite angles that also add to 180° must each be 90°, so only rectangles are cyclic.

quiz.q: In cyclic quadrilateral PQRS, ∠P = 95°. Side SR is extended beyond R. The exterior angle at R is:
quiz.explain: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle, ∠P = 95°. (∠R = 85°, and 180° − 85° = 95°.)
